segments.description: Welcoming Frederick Johansson to the Grand Same Coaches Conference. He studied at the Ghent University in Belgium from 2011 to 2017, receiving his PhD in sports science and sports medicine. His current position as a postdoctor at the Sophia Hammett University in Sweden, undertaking research in tennis and in medicine. He was the head of sports science at the Scandinavian College of manual medicine from 2007 to 2014 and has given more than 500 lectures in different sports on the topic of adolescent and sports performance and injury. His clinical experience over the last 20 years is within the area of sports medicine and fitness training. Currently, he is the senior lecturer in sports medicine at the Scandinavian College of manual medicine, director of the tennis research and performance group and serves on the board of the Society for Tennis Medicine and Science. Please welcome Frederick. Well, OK, thank you for the invitation. Scott Rawlins and tennis Australia. It certainly was a different one, not the usual that I used to get. So I really enjoyed that one. And well, after that email correspondence, I was brought into interrogation by Scott Rawlins himself. Well, it seems like I passed it because a few seconds later, the information just blew up and brought us to where we are at the moment. At the Tennis Australia Coaches Conference 2024, and it's a great pleasure to be here and share some thoughts with you.

On my topic, strength, the X-Factor Inserved Development, a unique prospective 10-year case study. My name is Frederick Johansson, associate professor at Sophia Hammett in Stockholm, Sweden. Also the Athletic Performance Director at Good to Great Tennis Academy and president for the Society of Tennis Medicine and Science, the STMS. The aim of this presentation is to present a pre-academic approach to serve development in the adolescent competitive tennis player. I want to share some evidence-based information, but also my experiences trying to develop the serve in a young player with regards to prevention, but also high performance. So it's quite a challenging task, and we'll see if we'll manage to go all the way through. This, I would call the development of the final product, mission possible, and hopefully not mission impossible. It's a presentation divided in three parts, setting the scene and moving between six and 12 years of age, adding some meat to the stew, and we're talking 13 to 16 years, and then finally the pre-academic approach, 17 to 19 years of age. So in part one, we try to set the scene, and by that I mean we want to be in the gym, in the fitness setting, but we also want to be on court. And for me, the trick is to combine these two, combine the training that we perform and try to transfer that on the court, and hopefully this will be some inspiration for you during the presentation.
